pedagogy.summary: 'Equally likely' means every outcome has exactly the same chance. The concept underpins the whole equally-likely model of probability (and the favourable-over-total formula that follows), so children must be able to decide whether a situation is fair — a coin, a balanced die, a spinner with equal sections — or not — a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with uneven sections. The crux is attending to the SIZE/number of each outcome region, not the number of different outcomes, and separating 'equally likely' from 'random'.
bestPractices: Contrast a spinner with equal sections against one with the same colours but unequal sections, so children see that equal chance depends on section size, not on how many colours there are
Use identical-face devices (coin, balanced die) to define equal likelihood by symmetry — the faces are interchangeable
Directly challenge 'two outcomes means 50-50' with a 1-red / 5-blue cube: two outcomes, but chances of 1/6 and 5/6
Distinguish 'equally likely' from 'random': an uneven spinner is still random, but its outcomes are not equally likely — sample repeatedly to show the unequal long-run pattern
Have children both identify and CREATE fair and unfair devices, explaining what makes each fair or not
keyRepresentations: Spinners: equal sections vs unequal sections (area = chance)
Fair coin and balanced die (identical, interchangeable faces)
Bags with equal vs unequal numbers of each colour
Area/region model in which equal chance corresponds to equal area
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that because there are two (or three) possible outcomes, they must be equally likely — counting the number of outcome types rather than their sizes
Equiprobability bias — believing any chance situation gives all outcomes an equal chance because the result is 'random/luck'
Judging a die or coin's fairness by how it is thrown or how well it is made, rather than by its identical faces (Watson & Moritz)
Confusing 'fair' as equal-chance with 'fair' as 'I have a good chance of winning'

learn.summary: Children learn that 'equally likely' means every outcome has exactly the same chance, decided by the SIZE/number of each outcome region rather than by how many different outcomes there are. They distinguish fair devices (balanced coin, balanced die, equal-section spinner) from unfair ones (bags with more of one colour, uneven spinners), confront the 'two outcomes means 50-50' trap, and separate 'equally likely' from 'random'.

activities.title: Build a fair three-colour spinner and test it by sampling
feedback: If a child eyeballs the wedges and one ends up bigger, point to the uneven tally: over many spins the biggest wedge tends to win most (though a small sample may not show this) — ask which section is larger and what that does to its chance.
When the three wedges are matched in size, highlight that the tally now evens out to roughly a third each (over many spins; small samples will vary).

For the 1-red / 5-blue case with six equal parts, if a child expected 50-50 'because there are two colours', show the tally landing near 1-in-6 for red: two outcomes, but very unequal chances (1/6 and 5/6).
Reinforce: equal chance is about equal size / number of equal ways, not the count of different colours.
activities.rationale: Because fairness is decided by region size, letting a child manipulate section size and then observe the long-run tally makes the deciding feature explicit and lets them test a wrong judgement empirically, which a fixed picture cannot support. The 1-red/5-blue case (six equal parts) directly challenges the 'two outcomes means 50-50' misconception.
sourceClaims: Having two outcomes does not make them equally likely: a cube with one red and five blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6 — equal chance requires the outcomes to be genuinely equal in number/size.
learnerActions: Try to divide a spinner into three colours (red, blue, green) so that each colour is equally likely to be landed on.
Spin the spinner many times (e.g. 100 times) and keep a tally of how often each colour comes up.

If one colour comes up clearly more often over many spins, examine the spinner: is one wedge bigger than the others? (Small differences in the tally can happen by chance even on a fair spinner.) Adjust the boundaries until the three wedges are the same size, checking the sizes directly, then spin and tally again.
State in your own words what makes the three colours equally likely — the equal AREA of each section, not the fact that there are three colours.
Then build the opposite: a cube with 1 red face and 5 blue faces (six equal faces), or a spinner split into six equal sections with 1 red and 5 blue; predict and then tally the long-run result.
Compare your prediction with the tally and explain why two colours did NOT give a 50-50 result.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal chance depends on each outcome region being the same size (or the same number of equal ways), not on how many different outcomes there are; sampling many times reveals equal-area regions producing roughly equal frequencies and unequal regions producing a lopsided tally.

activities.title: Sort and decide: fair or not fair?
feedback: If a child says the uneven three-colour spinner is fair 'because it has three colours', have them compare red against blue and green together: red covers as much as the other two combined, so it cannot have the same chance.
If a child says 'it's random, so every colour has an equal chance', note that an uneven spinner is still random yet lands on red far more often — random does not mean equally likely.
Praise reasoning that explicitly refers to equal size or equal counts rather than the number of colours.
activities.rationale: A categorisation task with carefully chosen contrasting cases surfaces whether the child reasons from region size/count or from the number of outcome types. This is a recognition task: a sort may check classification but does not itself elicit the child building a device or explaining it unprompted, so pair it with the construction activity.
sourceClaims: Having two outcomes does not make them equally likely: a cube with one red and five blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6 — equal chance requires the outcomes to be genuinely equal in number/size.
learnerActions: Look at a set of chance devices — spinners with equal and unequal sections, a balanced coin, a balanced die, bags with equal and unequal numbers of each colour.
Sort each device into 'equally likely outcomes' or 'not equally likely'.
For a spinner that has three colours but with red filling half and blue and green each a quarter, decide whether the three colours are equally likely and explain why or why not.
For each device, give the reason that decided your answer — equal section size or equal counts, not the number of different colours.
Answer the trap question: 'A cube has one red face and five blue faces — there are two colours, so does that make red and blue equally likely?' Explain why not.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding fair vs not-fair is a categorisation grounded in comparing the size or number of each outcome; the sharpest traps are the three-colour uneven spinner ('three colours so equal') and the two-outcome cube ('two outcomes so 50-50').

activities.title: Argue down the carnival host (equally likely vs random)
feedback: If the child accepts 'three colours so fair', prompt them to compare the sizes of the sections.
If the child conflates random with equally likely, ask: 'If we spun it 100 times, would the colours come up about the same? Why not?'
Confirm when the child names 'make the three sections the same size' as the fix.
activities.rationale: Arguing against an asserted-but-false claim can make the size-vs-count and random-vs-equal distinctions explicit through the child's own reasoning. A sampling demonstration can make the equal-area insight even more convincing, so combine with tallying where possible.
sourceClaims: The equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes of a random situation are equally likely — is a documented misconception; and Watson & Moritz found the large majority of children judged a die's equiprobability arbitrarily or attributed it to how well the die is made or how it is thrown rather than to its identical faces.
learnerActions: Listen to a carnival host who insists a spinner with a big red section is 'totally fair — three colours, three chances'.
Explain to the host why having three colours does not make the colours equally likely.
Point out that red's section is bigger than the others, so red is more likely.

Address the host's fallback claim that 'it's random, so you can't say one colour is more likely' — explain that the spin is random but the colours are still NOT equally likely because the sections differ in size.
Say what the host would have to change to make the spinner genuinely fair (three equal-sized sections).
activities.intendedInsight: Children can separate two ideas: an outcome being random (unpredictable on a single spin) versus outcomes being equally likely (same chance each). An uneven spinner is random but not equally likely.

activities.title: Why is a balanced die fair? (structure vs execution)
feedback: If a child attributes fairness to how hard the die is thrown, separate structure from execution: a balanced die has six identical faces and even weight, so no face is favoured; how hard you throw does not change which faces exist. If a child mentions how the die is made, agree that this matters: a die must be evenly made (not weighted) for its identical faces to give equal chances.
Reinforce that identical/interchangeable faces on an evenly weighted (balanced) die are what make the outcomes equally likely by symmetry.
activities.rationale: Watson & Moritz found many children judge a die's equiprobability by how it is thrown or made rather than by its identical faces; directly contrasting structure with execution targets this documented error. The tap-to-reveal comparison can present the definition but cannot let the child test a wrong judgement by sampling, so it works as a scaffold alongside the construction activity. A physical die, if used, can support the identical-faces insight without implying any medium is required.
sourceClaims: The equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes of a random situation are equally likely — is a documented misconception; and Watson & Moritz found the large majority of children judged a die's equiprobability arbitrarily or attributed it to how well the die is made or how it is thrown rather than to its identical faces.
learnerActions: Examine a balanced die and a fair coin: count the faces and check that the faces are identical/interchangeable.
Explain why each face of a balanced die is equally likely — because the six faces are identical in shape and size and the die is evenly weighted, so no face is favoured.
Answer the question: 'Is a die fair because of how hard you throw it, or because of something about the die itself?' Explain your reasoning.
Reveal and compare each section of a fair and an unfair spinner (its size and its chance), noting 'equal sections → equal chance'.
activities.intendedInsight: Fairness comes from the structure of the device (identical faces, equal-sized sections, and even weighting so that no face or section is favoured), not from how hard it is thrown.

constraints: Target the crux: equal chance is decided by the SIZE/number of each outcome region, not by how many different outcomes there are.
Explicitly separate 'equally likely' from 'random': an uneven spinner is still random but its outcomes are not equally likely.
Also distinguish the two senses of 'fair': equal-chance versus 'I have a good chance of winning'.

Sorting/categorisation is a recognition task: it may check classification but does not itself elicit the child independently building a fair device and explaining it; pair it with a construction task.
A static tap-to-reveal comparison can present the definition but cannot let the child test a wrong judgement by sampling; treat it as a scaffold, not the main mechanism.

Sampling (spinning many times and tallying) is what reveals that equal-area regions give roughly equal frequencies and imbalance gives a lopsided tally; keep this as the empirical check, noting small samples vary.

Optional interaction examples (dragging spinner-section boundaries, adding/removing counters in a bag, a 'spin many times' tally, highlighting equal vs unequal area) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a real 3D die as adding 'no conceptual leverage a 2D model lacks'. This comparative-efficacy claim is not established by the cited sources; a physical die can still support the structure-vs-execution insight (identical faces). Retained here as the structure-vs-execution activity without asserting any medium is unnecessary or superior.

The source assessment uses roughly 20 spins for Spinner Y (red half, blue/green quarters) and expects red near 10, blue and green near 5 each. These are expected-value approximations; small samples vary, so a single run may not match — frame tallies as 'about' these values and, where possible, use larger samples to make the long-run pattern reliable.
The 1-red/5-blue trap relies on six EQUAL parts/faces to give probabilities 1/6 and 5/6; a cube supplies this naturally, and any spinner version must use six equal sections.
Legacy confidence was 'high'; this rewrite does not independently upgrade or verify that rating.

assess.poeTask: Show Spinner Y (red half, blue quarter, green quarter). Ask: 'If I spin this 20 times, will the three colours come up about the same number of times, or not — and why?' Have the child predict AND give a reason before spinning. A child holding 'three colours, so about equal' predicts roughly equal thirds; spinning 20 times and tallying (red near 10, blue and green near 5 each) confronts the prediction and forces attention onto the differing section sizes.
probeDeeper: What would you have to change about Spinner Y to make its colours equally likely?
A cube has one red face and five blue faces. There are two colours — does that make red and blue equally likely? Why not?
If I spin the uneven spinner is the result still random? Is 'random' the same as 'equally likely'?
Is a balanced die equally likely because of how you throw it, or because of something about the die itself?
assess.correctAnswer: Spinner X. Its three sections are the same size, so red, blue and green each have an equal chance. On Spinner Y the red section is bigger — half the spinner — so red is more likely than blue or green. Both spinners have three colours, but equal chance depends on the sections being the same SIZE, which only X has.

errorPatterns.pattern: Number of outcome types implies equal likelihood — 'both spinners are fair because each has three colours'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the sections: red on Y covers as much as blue and green together, so it cannot have the same chance; ask what would make Y fair (three equal sections)
errorPatterns.distractor: Both spinners — each one has three colours, so each colour has an equal chance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks 'both' and reasons from the count of colours, ignoring that Y's red section is larger

errorPatterns.pattern: Equiprobability bias — 'both, it's random so every colour has an equal chance'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Spin Y many times and tally; red lands far more often even though each spin is random — separating 'random' from 'equally likely'
errorPatterns.distractor: Both — spinning is random, so you can't say one colour is more likely than another.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says both spinners give equal chances and appeals to randomness/luck rather than section size

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges fairness by the physical act or the make of the device rather than its structure (Watson & Moritz)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate structure from execution: a balanced die has six identical faces, so no face is favoured; how hard you throw does not change which faces exist
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked why a fair die's faces are equally likely, cites how it is thrown or how well it is made rather than the six identical faces

responseLevels.gap: Decides fairness by the number of colours or by 'it's random', with no reference to section size or equal counts; calls the uneven spinner fair
responseLevels.full: Correctly identifies fair vs unfair by equal SIZE (or equal counts) of outcomes, picks Spinner X and justifies by equal area, dismisses the 'three colours so equal' and 'it's random so equal' claims, and can construct a fair device and say why it is fair
responseLevels.partial: Recognises equal-section spinners and balanced coins/dice as fair, but slips on the two/three-outcome trap or attributes fairness to throwing/making the device; can identify clear cases but not justify by equal size across all cases

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show two spinners. Spinner X has three equal sections — red, blue, green. Spinner Y has the same three colours but red fills half the spinner and blue and green each fill a quarter. Ask: 'On which spinner are the three colours equally likely — and why?' Take the answer, then ask them to explain the reason fully (Tier 2).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands equal likelihood attends to section size and picks X, justifying by equal area; a child counting outcome types says 'both, each has 3 colours'; an equiprobability-biased child says 'both, it's random'. The Tier-2 reason — size versus number-of-colours versus luck — is the separator.

sources.claim: Having two outcomes does not make them equally likely: a cube with one red and five blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6 — equal chance requires the outcomes to be genuinely equal in number/size.

The equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes of a random situation are equally likely — is a documented misconception; and Watson & Moritz found the large majority of children judged a die's equiprobability arbitrarily or attributed it to how well the die is made or how it is thrown rather than to its identical faces.
